lesson.title: From Simplest Ratio to Real Molecule: Molecular Formula
lesson.summary: A molecular formula gives the true number of each atom in one molecule of a compound, found by comparing the compound's actual molar mass to the mass of its empirical formula.
lesson.body:
An empirical formula tells a chemist the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound, but many real molecules contain more atoms than that simplest ratio suggests. Acetylene, C2H2, and benzene, C6H6, share the exact same empirical formula, CH, yet they are very different molecules with very different molar masses. The empirical formula alone cannot distinguish between them. What is needed is one more piece of experimental information: the compound's actual molar mass, measured independently, for example, from the mass of a known volume of the compound's vapor.

The relationship between the two formulas is straightforward once the empirical formula and its formula mass are known. The molecular formula is always a whole number multiple of the empirical formula, so the actual molar mass of the compound must be that same whole number multiple of the empirical formula's mass. Dividing the compound's true molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives that multiplier, usually called n: n = molar mass of compound / empirical formula mass. Once n is found, every subscript in the empirical formula is multiplied by n to produce the molecular formula.

A classic worked example connects directly back to the empirical formula skill. Suppose a compound is found by combustion analysis to have the empirical formula CH2O. Its empirical formula mass is calculated the same way any molar mass is calculated: 12.01 + 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 30.03 g/mol. If a separate measurement shows the compound's actual molar mass to be about 180.16 g/mol, the multiplier is n = 180.16 / 30.03 = 6.00. Multiplying every subscript in CH2O by 6 gives the molecular formula C6H12O6, which is glucose, the same compound already examined for percent composition. This shows the whole chain of mole reasoning fitting together: percent composition data can lead to an empirical formula, and a separately measured molar mass then reveals the true molecular formula.

It is worth noticing that the multiplier n must always come out close to a whole number if the empirical formula and the molar mass measurement are both correct, since a real molecule cannot contain a fractional number of the empirical unit. If a calculation produces something like n = 5.98 or n = 6.03, rounding to the nearest whole number, 6, is appropriate, since the small deviation reflects normal rounding in the atomic masses and experimental molar mass rather than an error in the method.

Molecular formula determination is the point where a compound's identity finally becomes fully known from mass data alone, no structural guessing required. It depends completely on the empirical formula work that came before it and on the molar mass concept introduced earlier, and it sets up the next major skill, combustion analysis, which is the experimental technique most often used to generate the percent composition or mass data that these formula calculations start from in the first place.
